rows.title: Positive proportion conjecture for partitions into MSTD subsets
rows.record_statement: A **$k$-decomposition into MSTD subsets** is a partition of $I_r=\{1,2,\ldots,r\}$ into $k$ subsets, each having more pairwise sums than pairwise differences. **Positive proportion conjecture.** For any finite $k\ge 2$, the proportion of $k$-decompositions of $I_r$ into MSTD subsets is bounded below by a positive constant. This would extend the known positive-constant lower bound for $k=2$ and give a uniform abundance result for decompositions into any fixed finite number of MSTD subsets; the source does not establish the conjecture for general $k$.
rows.source: Hung Viet Chu, Noah Luntzlara, Steven J. Miller and Lily Shao, “Infinite Families of Partitions into MSTD Subsets”, arXiv:1808.05460 (2019).
rows.what_was_proved: PROVED (Chu-Luntzlara-Miller-Shao 2018, Conjecture 1.5): for every fixed k >= 2 there are c_k > 0 and R_k such that for all r >= R_k, at least a proportion c_k of the partitions of {1,...,r} into exactly k nonempty blocks have every block MSTD (|A+A| > |A-A|). The case k = 2 was proved earlier by Asada-Manski-Miller-Suh.

evidence.says: Theorem 1.4: “the probability that A is bi-MSTD is bounded below by a positive number”.
Archive record with no public attempts or comments.

caveats: Asymptotic in r: the proportion is 0 for small r, and the bound holds for r >= R_k.
The constants are astronomically small (log10 of 1/c about 3654 for k = 2); nothing is said about the true proportion or its limit.
k = 2 is due to Asada-Manski-Miller-Suh. The new ingredient is the antipodal modular k-colouring used as fringes; the rest is the Martin-O'Bryant/Zhao fringe method.
Significance modest. The prior-art search was bounded: arXiv abstract sweep, Semantic Scholar citers of the source (10) and of AMMS (12), web, ProbXiv and registries.

rows.title: The Jacobi-symbol conjecture for the integers $c_p$
rows.record_statement:
Let $p$ be an odd prime. For $\delta\in\{0,1\}$, define

$$
D_p^{(\delta)}(w)=\left|\left(\frac{j^2-k^2}{p}\right)+\left(\frac{jk}{p}\right)w\right|_{\delta\leqslant j,k\leqslant(p-1)/2}-\left|\left(\frac{j^2-k^2}{p}\right)\right|_{\delta\leqslant j,k\leqslant(p-1)/2}.
$$

For $p\equiv1\pmod4$, let $c_p$ be the positive odd integer whose existence is asserted by the preceding theorem through $D_p^{(0)}(w)=-w((p-1)c_p/2)^2$; for $p\equiv3\pmod4$, let $c_p$ be the positive odd integer whose existence is asserted through $D_p^{(1)}(w)=w(c_p\sum_{k=1}^{(p-1)/2}(\frac{k}{p}))^2$.

**Jacobi-symbol conjecture for $c_p$.** For any odd prime $p$,

$$
\left(\frac{p}{c_p}\right)=1,
$$

where $(\frac{p}{c_p})$ is the Jacobi symbol.

The conjecture is based on numerical values of $c_p$ listed in the source. The supplied text gives no resolution or proof, so its status remains open.
rows.source: Deyi Chen and Zhi-Wei Sun, “On determinants involving (j^2-k^2p) and (jkp)”, arXiv:2408.14401 (2024).
rows.what_was_proved: For every odd prime p, let c_p be the positive odd integer defined by Chen and Sun's determinant identities (D_p^(0)(w) = -w((p-1)c_p/2)^2 for p = 1 mod 4; D_p^(1)(w) = w(c_p sum_{k<=(p-1)/2}(k/p))^2 for p = 3 mod 4). Then the Jacobi symbol (p / c_p) = 1 (Chen-Sun, arXiv:2408.14401, Conjecture 1.1); existence and uniqueness of c_p are part of the formal statement.

closest_prior_read.citation: Chen–Sun, On determinants involving Legendre symbols, Conjecture 1.1

evidence.says: Archive record with no public attempts or comments.

caveats: Modest significance: the p = 1 mod 4 half uses a Ren-Luo-type Vandermonde reduction mod p; the new idea is in the p = 3 mod 4 half (c_p mod 4 via a Pfaffian sign congruence).
Orientation is (p / c_p) as in the source; (c_p / p) = 1 is false (e.g. p = 43, 47, 67).
Bounded prior-art search (arXiv API, partly rate-limited; web search; ProbXiv; OpenAlex 0 citations); Google Scholar not used.

rows.title: The Catalan triangle Laurent polynomial and positivity conjecture
rows.record_statement:
Let $n_1,\ldots,n_m,n_{m+1}=n_1$ be positive integers. For an integer $j$ and non-negative integers $a,r$ with $a\leqslant n_1$, consider

$$
\frac{1}{[n_m+a]}{n_1+n_m\brack n_1-a}^{-1}\sum_{k=a}^{n_1}[2k][k]^{2r}q^{jk^2-(r+1)k}\prod_{i=1}^{m}{n_i+n_{i+1}\brack n_i+k}.
$$

**Catalan triangle Laurent polynomial and positivity conjecture.** This expression is a Laurent polynomial in $q$, and it has non-negative integer coefficients when $0\leqslant j\leqslant m$. This is presented as a stronger version of Theorem and as a generalization of a conjecture attributed to Guo and Wang; the supplied span does not state whether it has since been resolved.
rows.source: Victor J. W. Guo and Xiuguo Lian, “Proofs of two conjectures on Catalan triangle numbers”, arXiv:1806.02685 (2018).
rows.what_was_proved: For positive integers n_1,...,n_m with n_{m+1}=n_1, every integer j, and nonnegative integers a, r with a <= n_1, the expression (1/[n_m+a]) [n_1+n_m choose n_1-a]_q^{-1} sum_{k=a}^{n_1} [2k][k]^{2r} q^{jk^2-(r+1)k} prod_{i=1}^m [n_i+n_{i+1} choose n_i+k]_q is a Laurent polynomial in q with integer coefficients, and its coefficients are nonnegative when 0 <= j <= m (Guo-Lian, arXiv:1806.02685, Conjecture 6.1; MathDB 381408 = 339461).

routes_refused: arXiv API: export.arxiv.org/robots.txt disallows all paths (main arXiv also disallows /api); no API query issued.
Google Scholar: robots.txt disallows /scholar; no search request issued. OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar and Crossref substitutes attempted.
MathDB: not checked per recorded automated-access refusal.
Journal DOI and author-hosted Guo–Lian PDF unavailable; publisher-body refusal for Li–Wang retained.

closest_prior_read.citation: Guo–Lian, Proofs of two conjectures on Catalan triangle numbers, Theorem 4.2 and Conjecture 6.1

evidence.says: Theorem 4.2 proves the same mixed cyclic Gaussian-binomial quotient is an integer Laurent polynomial for j∈{0,…,m}.
Guo–Wang study Laurent divisibility of related cyclic Gaussian-binomial sums and powers of q-integers.
Ji-Cai Liu verifies odd q-super-Catalan positivity and a stronger alternating-sum positivity theorem.

caveats: MathDB 339461 is a duplicate record of the same conjecture; count once, cite both ids.
The m>=2 reduction is Guo-Lian's own; the new content is the one-part case (positivity at j=0 via a positive Newton basis; all-j Laurentness via root-of-unity interpolation, near-routine).
Sharpness of 0<=j<=m is a written-proof supplement, not formalised.
Li-Wang (RACSAM 2026) full text unread (closed access); its reference list and abstract exclude overlap.

rows.title: Variance-optimal functions on trees are centered at a vertex
rows.record_statement:
Let $T$ be a tree and let $X$ be a variance-optimal function over $T$. For vertices $u,r\in V(T)$, write $d(u,r)$ for their graph distance.

**Tree characterization conjecture.** There exists a vertex $r$ such that, for every vertex $u\in V(T)$,

$$
|X(u)-X(r)|=d(u,r).
$$

Moreover, if $T$ is not a path, then $r$ may be chosen so that $d(r)\geq 3$.

The conjecture is proposed as a simple characterization of variance-optimal functions on trees and as a strengthening of the preceding structural result about hairs. The supplied text gives no resolution.
rows.source: Matthew Yancey, “Probabilistic and Geometrical Applications to Graph Theory”, arXiv:1705.09725 (2017).
rows.what_was_proved: Conjecture 1.4 of Yancey (every variance-optimal function on a tree is centred at a vertex r, with |X(u) - X(r)| = d(u, r) for all u, and r of degree at least 3 when the tree is not a path) is false. On an explicit tree with 34 vertices a feasible function has score 14892, while every vertex-centred function has score at most 14888 (the best centres are vertices 0, 2 and 7), so no variance-optimal function on this tree has a centre. Lean proves that an optimal function exists on the witness and that the first clause fails for every optimum, hence the negation of the whole conjecture. The result contradicts Lemma 19 of Farhadi, Louis, Singh and Tetali (arXiv:2003.05582v3), whose proof treats three sign choices as independent; on the witness the three moves change the variance by -1/289, -72/289 and -1/289 rather than giving the claimed gain of 71/289. Every tree with at most 18 vertices satisfies the conjecture (referee's unpublished computation).
caveats: Bounded literature and registry search only; no erratum or later paper on Lemma 19 of Farhadi-Louis-Singh-Tetali was found. The statement that every tree with at most 18 vertices satisfies the conjecture is an unpublished computation by the referee and is not kernel-checked. No claim that 34 vertices is minimal.

rows.title: Polynomial formulas for truncated total depth in ordered trees
rows.record_statement:
Let $n$ and $\ell$ be integers satisfying $n\geq \ell\geq 1$. Let $\operatorname{totalD}(n,k)$ denote the total quantity studied in the paper, and let $\operatorname{totalDTrunc}(n,k)$ denote its truncated version. For each $\ell$, let $a_{\ell}(n)$ and $b_{\ell}(n)$ be polynomials in $n$. **Polynomial-formula conjecture.** For all $n\geq \ell\geq 1$, \

$$
\operatorname{totalD}(n,2\ell-1)-\operatorname{totalDTrunc}(n,2\ell-1)=\frac{a_{\ell}(n)}{(n+2\ell+2)^{(2\ell-2)}}{2n \choose n-2\ell-1}
\
$$

 and \

$$
\operatorname{totalD}(n,2\ell)-\operatorname{totalDTrunc}(n,2\ell)=\frac{b_{\ell}(n)}{(n+2\ell+4)^{(2\ell-2)}}{2n+1 \choose n-2\ell-2}.
\
$$

 Here $a_{\ell}(n)$ and $b_{\ell}(n)$ have degree $2\ell-2$ and non-negative integer coefficients; the leading coefficient of $a_{\ell}(n)$ is $2\ell-1$, and the leading coefficient of $b_{\ell}(n)$ is $\ell$. The conjecture would provide a simplified expression for $\operatorname{totalDTrunc}(n,\ell)$, but the supplied text gives no resolution.
rows.source: Stoyan Dimitrov, Martin Minchev and Yan Zhuang, “BFS versus DFS for fixed-level targets in ordered trees”, arXiv:2404.05664 (2026).
rows.what_was_proved: For ordered trees with n edges and the depth-first-search scores totalD and totalDTrunc of Dimitrov, Minchev and Zhuang, for every l >= 1 there are polynomials a_l and b_l of degree 2l-2 with non-negative integer coefficients and leading coefficients 2l-1 and l such that, for all n >= l, totalD(n,2l-1) - totalDTrunc(n,2l-1) = a_l(n) C(2n, n-2l-1) / (n+2l+2)^(2l-2) and totalD(n,2l) - totalDTrunc(n,2l) = b_l(n) C(2n+1, n-2l-2) / (n+2l+4)^(2l-2), with rising factorials in the denominators. This is Conjecture 7.6 of arXiv v1. The proof is a binomial-sum enumeration of the score difference followed by a pairing argument for non-negativity. Lean also confirms that the quadratic coefficient of b_3 is 1133, where Table 3 of v1 prints 113.
caveats: The conjecture appears in arXiv v1 and is absent from v2 (10 July 2026); the journal text (SIAM J. Discrete Math. 40(4) 1913-1945, doi 10.1137/25M1760891) was not read, only its abstract, which matches v2. If the journal text proves the conjecture this result is not new; nothing found suggests that.

rows.title: The three-small-triangles conjecture for five points
rows.record_statement:
Call a triangle **small** if its area is at most $1/4$. Given five points in a triangle of unit area, consider the triangles determined by triples of the five points. **Three-small-triangles conjecture.** The five points determine at least three small triangles.

The claim would strengthen the preceding result, which guarantees only one small triangle. The source notes that three cannot be replaced by four for the displayed configuration; if true, the conjecture would imply corresponding lower bounds for larger point sets by averaging.
rows.source: Matthew Kahle, “Points in a triangle forcing small triangles”, arXiv:0811.2449 (2008).
rows.what_was_proved: For any triangle of area 1 in the plane and any five points of the closed triangle (not necessarily distinct), at least three of the ten unordered triples of the points span a triangle of area at most 1/4, where degenerate triples count with area 0. This is Kahle's three-small-triangles conjecture; three cannot be replaced by four. The proof is a case analysis on the midpoint subdivision with a determinant identity; the reduction from an arbitrary triangle to a standard one is proved in Lean.
caveats: Degenerate triples are counted as small, the convention forced by the source's use of Soifer's one-triangle theorem. Soifer's book chapter on the problem (Springer) was not read; it is understood to reprint the 2008 material. Bounded literature search only.

rows.title: Submultiplicativity conjecture for the primitive-set ratio function
rows.record_statement:
For $k>1$, let $Q(k)$ be the number of primitive subsets of $\\{1,2,\ldots,k\\}$ and define

$$
g(1)=1,\qquad g(k)=\frac{Q(k)}{Q(k-1)}-1.
$$

Thus $g(k)$ is the ratio of primitive subsets of $\\{1,2,\ldots,k\\}$ that contain $k$ to those that do not. **Submultiplicativity conjecture for $g$.** The function $g$ is submultiplicative in the following sense: if $(n,m)=1$, then

$$
g(nm)\leq g(n)g(m),
$$

and, for every prime $p$,

$$
g(p^{i+1})\leq g(p^i).
$$

These inequalities are proposed as conjectural improved upper-bound tools for the exponential growth constant associated with counting primitive sets. The supplied text gives no resolution of this conjecture.
rows.source: Nathan McNew, “Counting primitive subsets and other statistics of the divisor graph of \1,2, n\”, arXiv:1808.04923 (2020).
rows.what_was_proved: Let Q(k) be the number of primitive subsets of {1,...,k} (no element divides another; the empty set is counted, as in OEIS A051026) and g(k) = Q(k)/Q(k-1) - 1, with g(1) = 1. Then g(nm) <= g(n) g(m) for coprime n, m >= 1, and g(p^(i+1)) <= g(p^i) for every prime p and i >= 0. This is McNew's Conjecture 1. The proof uses an antichain-avoidance monotonicity lemma (an FKG-type correlation inequality) and two block reductions.
caveats: Modest: about a page using a correlation inequality; a specialist in correlation inequalities might find it quickly, but it is not a corollary of a published theorem. Bounded literature search only. The prior-work paragraph of the paper still refers to internal review files and should be tidied before external use.

rows.title: The balanced-partition conjecture for the $\mathsf a;q$-down-degree expectation
rows.record_statement:
Let $\mathsf a$ and $q$ be indeterminates. For a balanced partition $\lambda$, write $w=\lambda_1$ for its width, $\ell=\ell(\lambda)$ for its length, and $d=\gcd(w,\ell)$. Define

$$
W_{\mathsf a;q}(n)=\frac{1-\mathsf a q^{1+2n}}{1-\mathsf a q}q^{-n},\qquad [n]_{\mathsf a;q}=\frac{(1-q^n)(1-\mathsf a q^n)}{(1-q)(1-\mathsf a q)}q^{1-n}.
$$

For $x,y\in[\emptyset,\lambda]$ with $y\lessdot x$, if $y$ is obtained by deleting a cell in row $s$, set

$$
\operatorname{wt}(x,y)=W_{\mathsf a q^{\frac{w+\ell}{d}};q}\left(\frac{w(s-1)+\ell(|x|-1)}{d}\right).
$$

Define

$$
\operatorname{ddeg}_{\mathsf a;q}(x)=\sum_{y\lessdot x}\operatorname{wt}(x,y),
$$

with the sum over $y\in[\emptyset,\lambda]$, and

$$
R(\lambda\mid\mathsf a;q)=\sum_{x\in[\emptyset,\lambda]}W_{\mathsf a q^{\frac{w\ell}{d}};q}\left(\frac{\ell|x|}{d}\right),
$$

so that

$$
\mathbb E_{\mathsf a;q}(X)=\frac{\sum_{x\in[\emptyset,\lambda]}\operatorname{ddeg}_{\mathsf a;q}(x)}{R(\lambda\mid\mathsf a;q)}.
$$

**Balanced-partition product conjecture.** If $\lambda$ is balanced, then

$$
\mathbb E_{\mathsf a;q}(X)=\frac{\left[\frac{w\ell}{d}\right]_{\mathsf a q^{\frac{w+\ell}{d}};q}}{\left[\frac{w+\ell}{d}\right]_{\mathsf a q^{\frac{w\ell}{d}};q}}.
$$

This is an $\mathsf a;q$-analogue of the down-degree expectation formula. The source presents it as a conjecture for balanced partitions of arbitrary slope; no resolution is supplied.
rows.source: Jang Soo Kim, Michael J. Schlosser and Meesue Yoo, “Enumeration of standard barely set-valued tableaux of shifted shapes”, arXiv:2006.03253 (2020).
rows.what_was_proved: For every nonempty balanced partition (in the journal's sense: the upper left corner of each addable cell lies on the diagonal line), the a;q-weighted expectation of the down-degree statistic of Kim, Schlosser and Yoo equals the conjectured quotient of a;q-numbers, as an identity in the field of rational functions Q(a,q); the denominator is proved nonzero. This is Conjecture A.2. The proof is a telescoping corner identity. The formula fails for every unbalanced shape tested, so the hypothesis is needed.
caveats: 'Balanced' is read as in the journal version (upper left corner of each addable cell on the line); the arXiv wording is ambiguous. Bounded literature search only; Hopkins, Lazar and Linusson remark in print that they could not connect the conjecture to their methods.

rows.title: The minimum-fort-size conjecture for marginal observances
rows.record_statement:
Let $G$ be a graph. Write $\underline{f}(G)$ for the minimum fort size of $G$, let $\mathrm{MObs}(G;i)$ denote the marginal observance at step $i$, and let $\gamma_P(G)$ denote the power domination number. For a positive integer $k$, write $[k]=\{1,\ldots,k\}$. **Minimum-fort-size conjecture.** If

$$
\underline{f}(G)\geq 4,
$$

then

$$
\mathrm{MObs}(G;i)\geq 4
$$

for all $i\in[\gamma_P(G)]$. This asks whether the relationship between minimum fort size and marginal observances established for smaller minimum fort sizes extends to minimum fort size at least four; its status is not resolved in the source.
rows.source: Beth Bjorkman, Sean English and Johnathan Koch, “Cost-Benefit Analysis for PMU Placement in Power Grids”, arXiv:2601.19775 (2026).
rows.what_was_proved: The conjecture that minimum fort size at least 4 forces every marginal observance MObs(G;i), for i up to the power domination number, to be at least 4 is false. An explicit graph on 25 vertices, built from two copies of the Fano plane with two lines removed joined through a hub, has no fort of size at most 3, maximum observed-set sizes 11 and 14 with one and two sensors, and power domination number at least 3, so its second marginal observance is 3. (By the referee's computation the maximum observances are 0, 11, 14, 19, 25 and the power domination number is 4.) A generic random search over about 80 million graphs on 10 to 28 vertices found no counterexample; the witness comes from a structured construction.
caveats: No claim that 25 vertices is the smallest counterexample. Lean proves the power domination number is at least 3 (the exact value 4 is the referee's computation). The source is a 2026 arXiv preprint with no citing papers yet. The prior-work paragraph of the paper still refers to internal review files and should be tidied before external use.

rows.title: Linear-threshold conjecture for connected size Ramsey numbers of star matchings
rows.record_statement:
Let $nK_{1,p}$ be the disjoint union of $n$ copies of the star $K_{1,p}$, and let $K_{1,m}$ be the star with $m$ edges. The connected size Ramsey number $\hat r_c(G_1,G_2)$ is the minimum number of edges in a connected graph $G$ such that $G\to (G_1,G_2)$. **Linear-threshold conjecture.** There exists a positive constant $c$ such that for all positive integers $m$, $n$, and $p$ with $m\geq c(n+p)$, we have

$$
\hat r_c(nK_{1,p},K_{1,m})=n(m+p)-1.
$$

The conjecture proposes that the exact value established in the paper for the stronger condition $m\geq (n^2+2pn+n-3)/2$ remains valid once $m$ is merely linear in $n+p$.
rows.source: Fanghua Guo, Yanbo Zhang and Yunqing Zhang, “Matching-star size Ramsey numbers under connectivity constraint”, arXiv:2404.03175 (2024).
rows.what_was_proved: For all positive integers n, p, m with m >= 5(n+p), the connected size Ramsey number of n vertex-disjoint stars K_{1,p} (red) against a star K_{1,m} (blue) equals n(m+p)-1: the minimum number of edges of a finite connected simple graph every red/blue edge colouring of which contains a red nK_{1,p} or a blue K_{1,m}. This proves the linear-threshold conjecture of Guo, Zhang and Zhang with c = 5; the source had the formula only for m >= (n^2+2pn+n-3)/2. Lean proves both the upper bound by construction and the lower bound for every connected graph with fewer edges. The constant 5 is not optimised; no constant c <= 2/3 can work (referee's computation at (n,p,m) = (2,1,2)).
caveats: The constant 5 is not optimised. Bounded literature search only; the 2025 journal version still lists the conjecture as open. Two references the referee could not verify (arXiv:2606.04439, arXiv:2604.17356) were removed from the revised paper.
